name: Illinois

notes: Groceries: the 1% state grocery tax ended January 1, 2026. Cities and counties may impose a 1% local grocery tax by ordinance, and the RTA (Cook and collar counties) and Metro East district taxes on groceries continue. Home-rule sales taxes do not apply to groceries. Soft drinks and candy are taxed at the general rate, which is not counted here.

Personal care products: menstrual products are exempt through December 31, 2026, when the exemption ends unless extended, which is not taken out here; diapers and other grooming and hygiene products are taxed in full.
Barber and beauty services, laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).

Gasoline: most pump gasoline is gasohol (10% ethanol), taxed on 90% of its price from 2024 through 2028, so the state's 6.25% comes to 5.625%; whether local sales taxes use the same 90% base wasn't confirmed, so the full local rate is used. Per-gallon motor fuel taxes (state 48.3 cents, held there from July 1 to December 31, 2026 when Public Act 104-0468 suspended the yearly inflation increase, with the rate from January 1, 2027 not yet announced; Chicago 8 cents; several counties) are excise taxes, left out here.

Local taxes on restaurant food and drink and on alcohol are counted where a city publishes the rate (Chicago, Naperville, Rockford, Evanston; the local rates table names them and the ones not counted).

Hotel stays pay the state hotel operators' occupation tax (6% of 94% of receipts) instead of sales tax; Chicago adds its 4.5% hotel tax plus convention, sports facility, Cook County and other taxes (about 17.4% in all, as reported by the Civic Federation) and, since May 1, 2026, a 1.5% tourism district charge at hotels of 100 or more rooms in 17 central ZIP codes; none is counted here.
Tobacco is assumed taxed at the general rate (excise taxes left out); not verified state by state.

200 municipality or county parts list rates by address only (business districts inside them); their rate outside any business district, covering the most addresses, is used.
Rates include every tax that covers the whole municipality (county, municipal, home rule, transit). Business districts and other districts covering part of a municipality are not included.

Local restaurant and alcohol taxes are counted where the city's own page gives the rate: Chicago (0.5%, plus 1% in the McCormick Place tax area along the lake, and 1.5% on alcohol bought in stores), Naperville (1%), Rockford (1%, on alcohol too) and Evanston (6% on alcohol). Other suburbs with taxes on places for eating, among them Bensenville, Lombard, Clarendon Hills, Willowbrook, Gurnee, Itasca, Elburn, Brookfield, Buffalo Grove and Des Plaines, are not counted: their rates weren't checked.

1714000: Restaurant food and drink in Chicago carry the city's 0.5% restaurant tax, counted here, and, in the Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority's area from Diversey to the Stevenson Expressway east of Ashland, a 1% food and beverage tax, counted for the tracts whose center lies inside it (IDOR). The same 1% applies in two other areas, which aren't placed here: Midway Airport's square mile (55th to 63rd Streets, Cicero to Central Avenues) and a Northwest Chicago area around O'Hare bounded by York Road, Touhy Avenue, the Northwest Tollway, Lee Street, Higgins Road, Mannheim Road, Irving Park Road and the Cook-DuPage county line.

Chicago's 1.5% tax on alcohol bought for consumption off the premises (since March 1, 2026, in place of the per-gallon tax on those sales) is counted in its alcohol rate (City of Chicago). Drinks served in bars and restaurants keep the per-gallon tax paid by distributors, which isn't counted; the alcohol category doesn't separate them from bottles bought.
Not counted: Chicago's 3% tax on bottled and canned soft drinks (IDOR) and 9% tax on fountain drink syrup (Municipal Code 3-45), since the categories don't separate soft drinks.
1724582: Evanston's 6% Liquor Consumption Tax on prepared and packaged alcohol is counted in its alcohol rate. The city's page gives the combined rate on alcohol as 16.25%, which doesn't match its 10.5% general rate plus 6% (city of Evanston).
1751622: Naperville's 1% food and beverage tax is counted in its restaurant rate; a further 0.75% applies downtown, which isn't placed here (city of Naperville).
1765000: Rockford's 1% Redevelopment Fund Tax on food, drink and liquor, package liquor included, is counted in its restaurant and alcohol rates (city of Rockford).
1770122: Skokie levies a 2% restaurant tax, as reported in 2015 (Patch); it isn't counted here, since a current rate on the village's own pages wasn't found.
